facts.statement: Born in Southwark in 1861, the son of a railway clerk; educated at Cranleigh and Sandhurst, commissioned in Royal Marine Light Infantry in 1881 and transferred to Indian service in 1886.
Commanded a battalion of the Kashmir contingent at Gilgit and commanded the garrison at Chitral in 1895. CB and brevet major for Chitral, and a medal with two clasps in a contemporary account.
Commanded the 12th Sudanese Battalion in Egyptian service; fought at the Atbara and Khartoum in 1898, the year of his DSO. Major-general in 1911.

The British expedition protected the oil interests around the Persian Gulf. Townshend led the 6th (Poona) Division along the Tigris in 1915, took Amara and Kut, failed to break through at Ctesiphon and surrendered at Kut on 29 April 1916 after relief failed.
Townshend was a prisoner between 1916 and 1918. His captivity differed from the forced marches and deaths suffered by many men of the garrison.
KCB dated 1917 by the King’s College archive catalogue. After the war published My Campaign in Mesopotamia (1920) and represented the Wrekin, 1920–22. Died in 1924.

uncertainties.decision: The Liddell Hart Centre catalogue gives 1917. The original appointment notice and exact date have not been located. The 1916 defence report still styles him CB and DSO.
The contemporary Illustrated War News records two clasps. The named clasp combination needs a personal roll; none is asserted.

interpretation.note: Interpretation of the documented life and works; no claim of personal acquaintance from shared themes.

appraisal.note: AETERNUS editorial judgement; not presented as a historical quotation.

en.tagline: From the frontier fort at Chitral to the surrender on the Tigris.
en.intro: After Ctesiphon, Charles Townshend brought his depleted division back down the Tigris and stood at Kut. Twenty years earlier, a relief column had reached the fort he held at Chitral. At Kut, month after month, the force sent to relieve him failed to reach the town. By April 1916, surrender was all that remained to the commander.
en.orientation: Townshend, the son of a Southwark railway clerk, began in the Royal Marine Light Infantry and made his reputation in Indian service. Chitral brought the CB in 1895. He commanded Sudanese troops in the Egyptian Army, received the DSO in 1898 and rose to major-general in 1911. The 6th (Poona) Division put him at the head of the advance up the Tigris in 1915.
overview: The Mesopotamian expedition had begun around the Persian Gulf, where Britain sought to protect its oil supplies. From Amara and Kut the advance was carried towards Baghdad. After the fighting at Ctesiphon, it ended in retreat and a siege. On 29 April 1916 the British and Indian garrison surrendered. Townshend later published his account of the campaign.
origin: From Cranleigh and Sandhurst he went into the Royal Marine Light Infantry in 1881. He transferred to Indian service in 1886. At Gilgit he commanded the Raga Pertab battalion of the Kashmir contingent. His experience on the frontier preceded the six-week defence of Chitral in 1895.
career: In the Egyptian Army he commanded the 12th Sudanese Battalion and served in the fighting at the Atbara and Khartoum. Those were years in which British officers could make their careers across several armies of the Empire. Townshend’s wartime command of the 6th (Poona) Division, itself a formation of the Indian Army, belonged to that system.

The Tigris was the route of the advance and the line on which troops and supplies had to reach it. After Ctesiphon, the division went back to Kut. Hunger wore down the garrison while relief attempts failed. Townshend spent his captivity in conditions far removed from the forced marches and privations that killed many of the men he had commanded.
literature: My Campaign in Mesopotamia appeared in 1920. Townshend reconstructs what he knew, what he ordered and what he expected his superiors to do. His account stands beside the despatches he wrote during the siege and the letters of fellow prisoners. Read together, they give the decisions at headquarters and the price paid for them their different weight.
en.legacy: After the war he sat in Parliament for the Wrekin from 1920 to 1922. His account of the expedition remains a source for the predicament of a divisional commander. Its sharpest questions concern the further advance towards Baghdad, the means allotted to it and the decision to stand at Kut.
en.bridge: My Campaign in Mesopotamia follows the advance and siege through Townshend’s dispatches, recollections and judgments as the commanding officer.
en.description: Charles Townshend’s career from Chitral and the Sudan to the advance on Baghdad, surrender at Kut and My Campaign in Mesopotamia.

note.en: Military Division. Announced on 16 July for Chitral. The same notice records his separate promotion to brevet major, dated 10 July.
Awarded after the Sudan campaign. Contemporary notices still styled him CB and DSO at the time of the siege of Kut.

honours.name: Order of the Bath · Knight Commander (KCB)

note.en: The King’s College archive catalogue gives 1917 for this higher grade of the Bath.
A contemporary account records a medal with two clasps for the campaign.

en: The frontier garrison held for about six weeks in 1895 before relief reached the fort.
The town lies in a bend of the Tigris. The river was the artery of the campaign, and successive attempts to force a passage to the garrison failed.

connections.en: A senior commander at Kut whose letters document the siege and the fate of the prisoners.
Hutchinson took part in the Chitral relief; Townshend commanded the besieged garrison.
